metadata.title: Weight and Mass Are Not the Same Thing
metadata.register: formal, undergrad/grad audience, no casual narration, no doodle asides
metadata.branding: none — unbranded, book content only, no channel/logo/handle

beats.narration_text: The same astronaut weighs one hundred eighty pounds on Earth, but only thirty pounds on the Moon. Did she lose five sixths of her mass?
beats.new_visual_element: Short-only question card: the driving question appears centered on screen in ink text with a crimson underline, posed before any explanation begins.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: question card faded out, blank cream background

beats.narration_text: Here is the same astronaut, standing on a scale, once on Earth and once on the Moon. On Earth, the scale reads one hundred eighty pounds. On the Moon, it reads only thirty. Did she lose five sixths of her mass? Not even a little.
beats.new_visual_element: Two panels labeled EARTH and MOON, each with a figure standing on a scale. The Earth scale reads 180 lb. The Moon scale reads 30 lb.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: two labeled panels, figures on scales showing 180 lb and 30 lb

beats.narration_text: Weight is simply gravity's pull on an object. The force W equals mass times g. Change the planet, and g changes with it, so the weight arrow gets shorter. Weight is a force, and forces depend on where you are standing.
beats.new_visual_element: A crimson downward arrow appears on the Earth figure, labeled W equals m g, with g equals 9.8 beside it. On the Moon panel, the same arrow appears much shorter, labeled g equals 1.6.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: both panels show a downward crimson weight arrow, long on Earth, short on Moon

beats.narration_text: Now push her sideways instead of weighing her. That push has to overcome her mass, her resistance to being shoved around. And that resistance is exactly the same on the Moon as it is on Earth.
beats.new_visual_element: The weight arrows clear. In each panel, a teal arrow pushes a labeled block sideways, and the block slides the same distance, leaving a motion trail, on both Earth and Moon.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: both panels show a teal push arrow and a block that has slid an identical distance with a trail behind it

beats.narration_text: The push is identical, and so is the result: the same slide, the same distance, every time. There is no gravity involved in this comparison, and no friction to blame, just pure inertia, and inertia does not care which planet you are standing on.
beats.new_visual_element: Both slide trails are highlighted in gold, with a checkmark stamped over each panel and the words SAME RESISTANCE beneath.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: both panels show gold-highlighted trails, checkmarks, and the label SAME RESISTANCE

beats.narration_text: Weight and mass are proportional to each other, but they are not the same thing. Weight is how hard gravity pulls on you. Mass is how much you resist being pushed, anywhere in the universe.
beats.new_visual_element: A final held frame with two labels inside a gold-highlighted box: WEIGHT, a force that changes with gravity, and MASS, inertia that stays constant everywhere. The title above reads PROPORTIONAL, NOT THE SAME.
beats.accumulated_scene_state: final held frame: gold-highlighted box with the WEIGHT and MASS summary labels beneath the title
